name: Hip-Hop
blurb: From Bronx block parties to the charts: how rap and turntables changed pop.

questions.prompt: Which New York borough is regarded as the birthplace of hip-hop?
questions.fact: DJ Kool Herc threw an influential party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in August 1973, and many people date the movement from it.

questions.prompt: Which 1979 single by the Sugarhill Gang introduced many Americans to rap on the radio?
questions.fact: Record executive Sylvia Robinson put the trio together, and the track runs more than ten minutes in its full version.

questions.prompt: Which trio from Hollis, Queens, made the 1986 album Raising Hell?
questions.fact: Their song "My Adidas" led to a real endorsement deal with the sportswear company.

questions.prompt: Which trio's 1986 debut, Licensed to Ill, included "Fight for Your Right"?
questions.fact: The group began as a hardcore punk band in New York in the early 1980s.

questions.prompt: Which group, from Compton, California, released Straight Outta Compton in 1988?
questions.fact: The members included Dr. Dre, Ice Cube, Eazy-E, MC Ren and DJ Yella.

questions.prompt: Which Brooklyn rapper released the 1994 album Ready to Die?
questions.fact: The album came out on Sean Combs's Bad Boy Records, and the rapper's real name was Christopher Wallace.

questions.prompt: Which rapper had a 2002 hit with "Lose Yourself" from the film 8 Mile?
questions.fact: The song won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.

questions.prompt: Which rapper signed to Death Row Records after Suge Knight posted his bail in 1995, then recorded "California Love" with Dr. Dre?
questions.fact: Roger Troutman of Zapp sang the talk-box hook, and the video drew on the film Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome.

questions.prompt: Which group, led by Chuck D and Flavor Flav, released "Fight the Power" in 1989?
questions.fact: The song was written for Spike Lee's film Do the Right Thing.

questions.prompt: Which Atlanta duo of Big Boi and Andre 3000 won the 2004 Grammy for Album of the Year?
questions.fact: The winning album was Speakerboxxx/The Love Below, which includes the hit "Hey Ya!"

questions.prompt: The technique of moving a record back and forth under the needle to make rhythmic sounds is called what?
questions.fact: Grand Wizzard Theodore, a teenager in the Bronx, is often credited with discovering it in the 1970s.

questions.prompt: What is the title of the 1982 Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five hit that described life in the inner city?
questions.fact: Duke Bootee and Melle Mel wrote it, and its bleak picture of city life was a sensation.

questions.prompt: Which label did Rick Rubin and Russell Simmons found in 1984, starting in Rubin's college dorm room?
questions.fact: The label's early acts included LL Cool J, the Beastie Boys and Public Enemy.

questions.prompt: The Wu-Tang Clan, who recorded "C.R.E.A.M.," call which New York borough Shaolin?
questions.fact: The group took its name and style partly from Hong Kong martial-arts films.

questions.prompt: Dr. Dre's 1992 album The Chronic drew heavily on the sound of which funk collective?
questions.fact: The resulting laid-back, synthesizer-heavy style became known as G-funk.

questions.prompt: A Tribe Called Quest's "Can I Kick It?" is built on a sample from which Lou Reed song?
questions.fact: The Queens group's jazzy, relaxed style set it apart from the harder sound of the time.

questions.prompt: Run-DMC's 1986 hit "Walk This Way" was a remake of a 1975 song by which rock band?
questions.fact: Steven Tyler and Joe Perry joined Run-DMC for the recording, and the collaboration helped revive Aerosmith's career.

questions.prompt: What do the letters LL stand for in LL Cool J's stage name?
questions.fact: The rapper was born James Todd Smith in Queens, and he signed to Def Jam as a teenager.

questions.prompt: Which Salt-N-Pepa song of 1987 began life as a B-side?
questions.fact: DJs began playing the B-side, and it turned the trio into stars.

questions.prompt: Which N.W.A member left the group in 1989 over money and released AmeriKKKa's Most Wanted in 1990?
questions.fact: Dr. Dre left in 1991 and co-founded Death Row Records.

questions.prompt: At his 1973 Bronx party, DJ Kool Herc used two copies of the same record to extend what part of a funk song?
questions.fact: He called the technique the Merry-Go-Round, and dancers who waited for the break became known as b-boys and b-girls.

questions.prompt: Public Enemy's dense, layered productions were created by a team known as what?
questions.fact: The Bomb Squad built tracks from dozens of small samples, which made Public Enemy's records sound urgent.

questions.prompt: Which poet and musician's 1970 spoken-word piece "The Revolution Will Not Be Televised" is often cited as an influence on rap?
questions.fact: Scott-Heron performed over spare conga and bass accompaniment, and he later recorded for Arista.

questions.prompt: The Notorious B.I.G.'s "Juicy" samples which R&B group's "Juicy Fruit"?
questions.fact: Mtume's slow, smooth 1983 song supplies the track's hook.

questions.prompt: Coolio's "Gangsta's Paradise" builds on which Stevie Wonder song?
questions.fact: Wonder reportedly agreed to the sample only after the lyrics were changed to remove profanity.

questions.prompt: Which record executive passed Eminem's demo tape to Dr. Dre?
questions.fact: Dre has said he was struck by the tape immediately, and he went on to produce much of Eminem's early work.

questions.prompt: Before his own albums, Kanye West produced tracks for which rapper's 2001 album The Blueprint?
questions.fact: West's soulful, sped-up samples helped define the album's sound.

questions.prompt: OutKast's "Ms. Jackson" was inspired by the mother of which singer?
questions.fact: Andre 3000 wrote the song after the end of his relationship with Badu, with whom he had a son.

questions.prompt: Jay-Z grew up in which Brooklyn housing project?
questions.fact: The Marcy Houses are in the Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhood, and he refers to the place often in his songs.

questions.prompt: Sugar Hill Records founder Sylvia Robinson had a 1973 hit as a singer with which song?
questions.fact: She founded the label after a career in R&B, and "Rapper's Delight" was among its first releases.

stories.title: A Party in the Bronx
stories.dek: Two turntables, a back-to-school dance and a new music
stories.body:
In the early 1970s the South Bronx was a place of hardship. Fires had destroyed whole blocks, the Cross Bronx Expressway had cut through old neighborhoods, and many families were struggling. Young people had few places to go. But they had music, and they had each other.

On August 11, 1973, a teenager named Clive Campbell, who went by the name DJ Kool Herc, helped his sister Cindy throw a back-to-school party in the recreation room of their apartment building at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue. Campbell had been born in Jamaica and moved to the Bronx as a boy. He brought with him the idea of the sound system, a powerful setup that Jamaican DJs used for street parties. He had two turntables and a big speaker rig.

Herc noticed something about the records he played. The part dancers liked most was the short instrumental "break," where the vocals dropped out and the drums took over. He found that with two copies of the same record he could switch back and forth and extend the break as long as he liked. He called the dancers who waited for it "break-boys," a name that gave rise to breakdancing. Herc also spoke over the music, calling out names and rhythms. That was the beginning of rapping.

Others took up the idea. Afrika Bambaataa, a former gang member, formed the Universal Zulu Nation to steer young people toward music and dance. Grandmaster Flash perfected a style of quick mixing, and his friends took turns at the microphone. Grand Wizzard Theodore, a teenager, is often credited with discovering scratching.

For years the music stayed local. In 1979 a New Jersey record executive, Sylvia Robinson, put together a group called the Sugarhill Gang for "Rapper's Delight." It was a hit and showed that the sound could sell. In 1982 Afrika Bambaataa's "Planet Rock," which used electronic sounds borrowed from the German band Kraftwerk, brought hip-hop together with synthesizers.

What started in a Bronx rec room became a worldwide art form. The party on Sedgwick Avenue is often celebrated as its birthday, and New York State later recognized the building as a historic site.

stories.title: Walk This Way
stories.dek: A rock band, a rap group and a wall that fell
stories.body:
By 1986 Run-DMC was one of the most successful rap groups in America. Joseph "Run" Simmons, Darryl "DMC" McDaniels and Jason "Jam Master Jay" Mizell came from Hollis, Queens. They wore black hats, leather jackets and Adidas sneakers without laces. Their records on Def Jam, such as "Rock Box," had already shown that rap and rock guitars could work together.

Producer Rick Rubin had an idea. He was a fan of both rock and rap, and he wanted to put them together. He suggested that the group record "Walk This Way," an Aerosmith song from 1975. Run and DMC did not know the lyrics well. They have said they thought the words were strange and were reluctant at first. But Jam Master Jay had been playing the song's opening drum beat as a DJ, and he understood why it worked.

Rubin invited the members of Aerosmith, Steven Tyler and Joe Perry, to the studio. At that point the band's career was in a slump. Perry's guitar and Tyler's voice, set against the rappers, gave the new version a punch that neither side could have produced alone. The result was a hit, and the video made it a landmark. In it, Run-DMC and Aerosmith perform in adjoining rooms until Tyler, singing, breaks through the wall that separates them.

The video was played constantly on MTV, which had been slow to show rap. Suddenly it gave the music a huge new audience. Many rock fans first heard hip-hop through that clip. For Aerosmith, it started a comeback that continued with their 1987 album Permanent Vacation.

The same year, Run-DMC released the album Raising Hell, which also included "My Adidas." The song was so popular that the sportswear company signed the group to an endorsement deal, an unusual step for a rap act at the time.

The collaboration crossed a line that many had thought uncrossable. Rock and rap, once seen as opposites, shared a sense of attitude and noise. After "Walk This Way," groups of all kinds mixed the two, and the combination has never stopped being used.

stories.title: Straight Outta Compton
stories.dek: A record the radio would not play and a letter from the FBI
stories.body:
In the late 1980s Compton, a city in Los Angeles County, was known for gang violence and tough living. Five young men there, Dr. Dre, Ice Cube, Eazy-E, MC Ren and DJ Yella, formed a group called N.W.A. They wanted to describe what they saw, without softening it.

Eazy-E put up the money to start Ruthless Records. Dr. Dre produced the music, and Ice Cube wrote many of the lyrics. In 1988 they released the album Straight Outta Compton. Its title track introduced the group to a national audience, with hard-edged beats and unflinching words about police and street life. Another song, an angry protest about police treatment of young Black men, drew the most attention.

The record received almost no radio play, and MTV did not show the group's videos. Yet it sold more than a million copies, mostly through word of mouth and in stores. Teenagers across the country, many of whom had never been to Los Angeles, bought it. In August 1989 an official at the FBI wrote a letter to the group's record company expressing concern about the song. The letter was widely reported, and it did more to publicize the album than any advertisement could.

The group did not last. In 1989 Ice Cube left over money and began a solo career, releasing AmeriKKKa's Most Wanted in 1990. Dr. Dre left in 1991 after disputes and co-founded Death Row Records. Eazy-E died of complications from AIDS in 1995.

Dr. Dre's next move changed rap again. His 1992 album The Chronic introduced a smoother, more melodic style built on the sounds of Parliament-Funkadelic. It was called G-funk. The single "Nuthin' but a 'G' Thang," with a young rapper named Snoop Doggy Dogg, became a hit and made West Coast hip-hop a national force.

N.W.A's first album remains a milestone. It showed that a rap record could succeed without help from the usual gatekeepers, and for a time it shifted the center of hip-hop from New York toward Los Angeles.

stories.title: The South Has Something to Say
stories.dek: OutKast at the Source Awards, August 1995.
stories.body:
In 1995 hip-hop was in the middle of a bitter rivalry between the East Coast and the West Coast. Labels, artists and fans were choosing sides, and the Source Awards, held in New York on August 3, were expected to be a showcase for both. The tension in the room was high before the show began, and artists from the two sides were said to be watching each other warily.

Into this scene came two young rappers from Atlanta, Andre 3000 and Big Boi, who made up the duo OutKast. Their debut album, Southernplayalisticadillacmuzik, had been out for a little over a year. It was not like the hard-edged East Coast or West Coast records of the time. It had a slower, more melodic groove, and the lyrics were full of Southern slang and detail. The Source named them best new rap group of the year.

When they went up to accept the award, the audience booed. Many people in the New York crowd did not know the group's music, and some felt that a Southern act did not belong in the conversation. Andre 3000 took the microphone, and he spoke calmly and directly. He told the audience that the South had something to say. It was a short statement, but it was a kind of declaration of independence.

The same evening had its own dramas. Suge Knight, head of Death Row Records, made a pointed remark about rival executives, which fed the feeling of conflict. The feud between the two coasts grew sharper in the following months and years.

OutKast did not respond with anger. They answered with music. Their next albums, ATLiens, Aquemini and Stankonia, showed a creativity that few other groups could match. Stankonia, released in 2000, included Ms. Jackson, a song that blended funk, rap and pop, and it brought them a worldwide audience.

Andre 3000's words at the Source Awards are often remembered as a turning point. Within a few years, Southern hip-hop was one of the dominant forces in the genre, with artists from Atlanta, Houston, Memphis and New Orleans leading the way. The booing that night looks different now, as a sign of how much the audience had to learn.

stories.title: Tupac at Coachella
stories.dek: A digital image and a surprise guest list in the California desert.
stories.body:
In April 2012 Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg performed a set on the final night of the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival in California. They were two of the biggest names in West Coast hip-hop, and the crowd was ready for a night of classics. What it got was a moment that people kept talking about for years.

Partway through the set, the stage went dark. Then a figure appeared, shirtless, in jeans, and with a familiar swagger. It was Tupac Shakur, who had died in 1996. The image was not a real hologram. It was a projection, created by a visual effects company working with a technique similar to an old stage illusion, and it was displayed on a transparent screen so that it seemed to stand on the stage. The figure addressed the crowd and then performed two songs, Hail Mary and 2 of Amerikaz Most Wanted, with Snoop Dogg joining in.

The audience's reaction was a mix of awe and unease. Some fans cheered wildly, while others found it strange to see a man who had been dead for fifteen years on a stage in front of them. Within days, people around the world were debating whether it was a tribute or a trick. Some wondered whether it opened the door to other digital performances.

The show was also a reunion of the West Coast scene. Snoop Dogg and Dre performed songs from their careers, including Nuthin' but a G Thang, one of the signature tracks of the early 1990s, and they were joined by guests. Reports of the night list Eminem, 50 Cent and Kendrick Lamar among them, along with other friends and former collaborators. California Love, the song that paired Tupac and Dre in 1995, hung over the evening.

The image of Tupac was used again on the second weekend of the festival. Talk of a tour followed, but it never happened.

Whatever you think of the technology, the moment says something about Tupac's place in popular culture. Even years after his death, he was still the one the crowd wanted to see. Coachella gave his fans one more version of him.

covers.title: Walk This Way
covers.note: Aerosmith released it on Toys in the Attic in 1975. Run-DMC reportedly did not know the song at first, and Steven Tyler and Joe Perry joined the recording.

covers.title: Whatta Man
covers.note: Linda Lyndell recorded What a Man for Stax's Volt label in 1968. The 1993 version, with En Vogue singing the hook, reached the US top ten.

covers.title: Killing Me Softly with His Song
covers.note: Lori Lieberman recorded the Charles Fox and Norman Gimbel song in 1972, and Roberta Flack's 1973 version was the big hit. The Fugees' 1996 version reached number one in the UK.

covers.title: No Woman, No Cry
covers.note: Marley released a studio version on Natty Dread in 1974, crediting the song to his friend Vincent Ford. The Fugees put their version on The Score.

covers.title: Mary, Mary
covers.note: Michael Nesmith wrote it, and the Monkees released it in 1967 on More of the Monkees. Run-DMC recast it as a hard-edged track for Tougher Than Leather.

covers.title: I Feel for You
covers.note: Prince released it on his 1979 self-titled album. Khan's 1984 version added a rap by Melle Mel and a harmonica part by Stevie Wonder.

covers.title: Just the Two of Us
covers.note: Grover Washington Jr. released it on Winelight in 1980, with Bill Withers singing. Smith kept the hook and added new verses about his son.

covers.title: Lean on Me
covers.note: Withers released it on Still Bill in 1972. Club Nouveau's new jack swing version reached number one in the US, as Withers's original had.
